subject: operating-systems
title: Process creation and scheduling context
summary: Process creation establishes an execution context, after which the scheduler chooses among runnable processes or threads.

questions.prompt: What does a process control block (PCB) primarily store?
options: Metadata and saved execution state for a process
The contents of every disk block
questions.answerKey: A PCB records identity, state, registers, scheduling information, and resource references.
questions.explanation: Program code is stored separately from the bookkeeping structure.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a context switch?
options: To save one execution context and restore another
questions.answerKey: A context switch changes the CPU from one runnable context to another.
questions.explanation: It has overhead because registers and scheduler state must be handled.

questions.prompt: A parent creates a child and both are runnable. What determines which runs first?
options: A universal rule that children always run first
The scheduler policy and current system state
questions.answerKey: Scheduling policy, priorities, readiness, and timing determine dispatch.
questions.explanation: Many systems make no portable first-run guarantee.

questions.prompt: Why can frequent context switching reduce throughput?
options: Switching consumes CPU time without directly advancing application work
questions.answerKey: Context-switch work is overhead that could otherwise execute useful instructions.
questions.explanation: The size of the effect depends on workload and implementation.

questions.prompt: What information must an OS retain so a preempted process can resume correctly?
questions.answerKey: It must retain the process identity and state, program counter, CPU registers, stack pointer, address-space information, and scheduling/resource metadata sufficient to restore execution.
questions.explanation: A PCB is the usual abstraction for this saved context and metadata.

questions.prompt: Explain why process isolation usually costs more for communication than threads sharing one process.
questions.answerKey: Separate processes have separate address spaces, so communication generally needs IPC mechanisms and copying or shared-memory setup with explicit synchronization. Threads can directly access shared memory, reducing setup and copying but increasing synchronization and fault-sharing risks.
questions.explanation: Shared memory between processes is possible but must be explicitly established and protected.
